record.original_question: How can one explain this phenomenon that the Euler class in H 2n (Homeo0 (S2n−1 )) is unbounded but it vanishes on amenable subgroups?

evidence.quote: Question 3.15. How can one explain this phenomenon that the Euler class in H 2n (Homeo0 (S2n−1 )) is unbounded but it vanishes on amenable subgroups?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $n \geq 1$ and let $\mathrm{Homeo}_0(S^{2n-1})$ denote the identity component of the group of orientation-preserving homeomorphisms of the $(2n-1)$-sphere, regarded as a discrete group. Consider its (real) group cohomology $H^{2n}(\mathrm{Homeo}_0(S^{2n-1}); \mathbb{R})$, in which the Euler class $e_n \in H^{2n}(\mathrm{Homeo}_0(S^{2n-1}); \mathbb{R})$ is defined as the obstruction class for the universal $S^{2n-1}$-bundle.

Two phenomena are known:
(a) The class $e_n$ is unbounded, i.e., it does not lie in the image of the comparison map $H_b^{2n}(\mathrm{Homeo}_0(S^{2n-1}); \mathbb{R}) \to H^{2n}(\mathrm{Homeo}_0(S^{2n-1}); \mathbb{R})$ from bounded cohomology.
(b) For every amenable subgroup $A \leq \mathrm{Homeo}_0(S^{2n-1})$, the restriction of $e_n$ to $H^{2n}(A; \mathbb{R})$ vanishes.

Provide a conceptual explanation reconciling (a) and (b): namely, find a structural or cohomological mechanism that forces the Euler class to vanish on every amenable subgroup despite its non-boundedness on the full group.
artifact.status_search_result: No source was found that resolves the apparent paradox of the Euler class in $H^{2n}(\mathrm{Homeo}_0(S^{2n-1}))$ being unbounded yet vanishing on all amenable subgroups. Related results address bounded Euler classes for circle actions and vanishing of bounded cohomology for amenable groups, but no conceptual explanation of this specific phenomenon is documented; the question appears to remain open.

status_evidence.title: Bounded cohomology of discrete groups
status_evidence.snippet: Bounded cohomology of amenable groups vanishes for a wide class of coefficients.
status_evidence.claim: Vanishing of bounded cohomology on amenable groups is a general principle, but does not by itself explain why the (unbounded) Euler class restricts trivially to amenable subgroups.

status_evidence.title: An algebraic criterion for the vanishing of bounded cohomology
status_evidence.snippet: Criteria for vanishing of bounded cohomology in transformation groups.
status_evidence.claim: Recent work studies vanishing of bounded cohomology classes but does not resolve the specific phenomenon for $\mathrm{Homeo}_0(S^{2n-1})$.
